sentences.text: Mendozasaurus was a medium to large-sized titanosaur, a type of sauropod dinosaur, measuring between 18 and 30 meters in length.
Unlike other sauropods, this animal had a relatively robust neck base due to cervical neural spines shaped like fans that were wider than the vertebral centers.
The creature also possessed large bony plates up to 20 centimeters long running along its back.
Comparative studies suggest Mendozasaurus had a phalangeal formula of 2-2-2-2-0 based on a complete right foot.
Mendozasaurus is the first dinosaur discovered in Mendoza Province, Argentina.
Holtz estimated the length of Mendozasaurus at 22 meters.
In 2010, Gregory S. Paul estimated Mendozasaurus to be 20 meters long and weigh 16 tonnes.
Remains of Mendozasaurus were discovered and excavated by Bernardo Javier González Riga in southern Malargue, Mendoza Province, between 1998 and 2011.
Mendozasaurus remains come from a single locality known as Arroyo Seco in the Coniacian Sierra Barrosa Formation.
The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — includes articulated caudal vertebrae, several cervical vertebrae, one dorsal vertebra, and numerous disarticulated limb bones.
The name Mendozasaurus means "the first great reptile of Mendoza," combining Spanish, Greek, and Huarpe linguistic roots.
Mendozasaurus likely moved in herds near large rivers, with its carcasses later exposed to scavengers and episodic floods.
A 2018 analysis by González Riga et al. placed Mendozasaurus as the most basal member of the clade Lognkosauria.
Calvo et al. found Mendozasaurus to be a member of Titanosauridae or Lithostrotia, closely related to Futalognkosaurus.
Mendozasaurus lived between 89 and 86 million years ago during the Coniacian stage of the Late Cretaceous in South America.
More precisely, the animal lived from 89.8 to 85.7 million years ago during the Coniacian stage.
Mendozasaurus lived during the Cretaceous period on southern landmasses.
Mendozasaurus lived in environments of meandering rivers, wide floodplains, and conifer forests alongside freshwater turtles and carnivorous dinosaurs.
A 2022 study by Navarro et al. proposed an alternative phylogeny placing Mendozasaurus as more derived within the group, alongside Austroposeidon.
